comments.author: @Role-Play_Gamer
comments.text:
I am a writer and an artist. Producing something substantial, like an anime, is way less about skill than it is about having millions of dollars worth of resources at your disposal. A colorless manga/comic series is possible, but if you're creating it yourself, you're not gonna get that far without spending 20 hours a day drawing. What's important to me is the quality of the final product, not how it was created. If AI will be able to one-shot my style, that is massive for me.

AI tools are a dream come true for those with a passion to create, and a nightmare for those who create primarily for the fame or fortune and fear competition. You can't slice it any other way. If someone is actually passionate about going through the traditional process, they should have no beef with others using AI. The only thing AI users get in the way with is competition. And protesting others' creativity for the sake of staying ahead is just plain arrogance.

And when it comes to replicating popular artstyles, I have done that in the past and it was well received. But now that AI is the one doing it, people label it as stealing? Most don't get that AI learns art similar to how humans do; they look at images and learn general patterns, resulting in both the ability to replicate styles, as well with come up with new styles by mixing what they've learned.

comments.text:
There's definitely a paradox when artists who pride themselves on imagination and boundary-pushing seem reluctant to explore the philosophical frontiers that AI opens up.

AI does introduce fascinating questions that could be rich territory for artistic exploration. 

These are profound philosophical questions about art, consciousness, and human experience that creative thinkers could be engaging with directly through their work with AI. Simply creating "an AI song" might be limiting, but using AI to interrogate deeper questions about creativity itself could be revolutionary.

There is something ironic about creative people who have built careers on innovation and pushing boundaries being reluctant to engage with one of the most significant technological and philosophical shifts of our time. The truly imaginative response might be to dive into these tensions and contradictions rather than avoid them.

Some artists are embracing this challenge, using AI not just as a tool but as a philosophical collaborator that helps them explore new dimensions of what creativity and art can be. That approach seems more aligned with the spirit of artistic innovation than categorical rejection.

comments.text:
Most people are focused on what AI produces—but the real artistic potential is in AI itself as the artwork. The model, the training data, the logic it’s built on—that’s the art. Not the image it spits out, but the system you design: a living, evolving creative entity. It’s not about mimicking human art, it’s about exploring a new kind of creativity that doesn’t need to be human at all.

AI as artwork flips the whole game. Instead of just using AI to make a cool picture or song, the REAL art is the AI system itself. Artists designing custom datasets, training unique models, and shaping how they learn - that's the creative act.

Think about it: painters don't just make paintings, they develop unique approaches and styles. Now artists can literally design intelligence with its own aesthetic perspective.

Helena Sarin, Anna Ridler, and Mario Klingemann are already exploring this - they're less focused on specific outputs and more on creating systems with interesting behaviors and tendencies.

It's like moving from judging a painting to appreciating an entire creative mind. The outputs are just glimpses of the real artwork: the artificial intelligence itself, with all its quirks and capabilities. That's the true frontier of creative expression with AI.
